explanations.explanation: Spring it is, friend. The prophet tells Ahab, Israel's king, “Go and strengthen your position, and take note what you must do, for in the spring the king of Aram will come up against you.” That's a warning with a season stamped right on it. Then verse 26 rolls around and Ben-hadad, Aram's king, shows up on schedule.

Winter is a fair guess. Nobody wants to march anywhere when it's cold, and I'd stay home too. But the prophet says spring, not winter. In verse 26 Ben-hadad, king of Aram, mobilizes the Arameans in the spring, just like the prophet said.

Fall sounds like a nice time for a battle, if you like crunchy leaves. But the prophet tells Ahab, Israel's king, that the king of Aram will come up against him in the spring. The text never mentions fall. Verse 26 says Ben-hadad mobilizes the Arameans in the spring.

The plains, friend. Ben-hadad's servants say, “Their gods are gods of the hills. That is why they prevailed over us.” So they say they should fight on the plains, where they think they will surely prevail. They've got a whole plan built on that idea.

I see why you'd think mountains, since the servants are talking about hills. But they want to stay away from the hills. They say, “we should fight them on the plains; surely then we will prevail.” The plains are where they want the next fight.

Sand, waves and a battle sounds like a lot of work. The seashore never comes up in this passage, though. The servants of Ben-hadad, Aram's king, say the fight should be on the plains. That's the whole plan, in verse 23.

explanations.answer: One just like the army he lost
explanations.explanation: Right on target. The servants say to raise an army “like the one you have lost,” and then spell it out: horse for horse and chariot for chariot. It's a copy of the old army, just on a new battlefield. Nobody says anything about making it bigger or fancier.

explanations.answer: One twice the size of the last
explanations.explanation: Double sounds impressive, I'll give it that. But the servants don't ask for more. They say to raise an army “like the one you have lost,” horse for horse and chariot for chariot. Same size, new location.

explanations.answer: A smaller army that moves faster
explanations.explanation: A small and speedy army is a fun idea, but it isn't in the text. The servants ask for an army “like the one you have lost.” That means horse for horse and chariot for chariot, a swap for what Aram already lost. Nothing in verse 25 says smaller.
This one's easy to flip, so no worries. The text says the opposite. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, approves the plan and acts accordingly (1 Kings 20:25). He doesn't push back at all.
That's it. The text says, “the king approved their plan and acted accordingly.” Ben-hadad is king of Aram, and his servants say jump, so he jumps. No arguing, no second guessing.
Aphek is the place. Verse 26 says Ben-hadad mobilized the Arameans and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. Remember that name, friend, because Aphek comes back later in this very passage.
Megiddo is a name worth knowing, but it isn't in this passage. The text says Ben-hadad, king of Aram, went up to Aphek. That's where the Arameans gather to fight Israel.
Jezreel doesn't show up here. This passage names Aphek as the place Ben-hadad, Aram's king, goes up to fight against Israel (1 Kings 20:26). Stick with the name the text gives us.

That's the picture. The Israelites camp like two small flocks of goats, while the Arameans cover the countryside. Count that gap, friend. A couple of little flocks on one side and the whole landscape on the other.

explanations.answer: It fits in one small valley
explanations.explanation: Small valley would be the Israelite side of things. The text says they camp like two small flocks of goats. The Arameans are the other way around, because they cover the countryside.
The seashore never comes up in this passage. The text says the Arameans cover the countryside, while the Israelites are like two small flocks of goats. So it's a land that's full of Arameans.

explanations.answer: Deliver their great army into Ahab's hand
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. The man of God says, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because the Arameans have said that the LORD is a god of the hills and not of the valleys, I will deliver all this great army into your hand.’” The Arameans said it, and the LORD answers it. He gives the whole great army to Ahab, Israel's king.

explanations.answer: Let the Arameans win on the plains
explanations.explanation: That's what the Arameans are hoping for, but it's the opposite of what the LORD says. Because of what they said about Him, He says, “I will deliver all this great army into your hand.” The hand belongs to Ahab, Israel's king. The plains plan is not going to go the way Ben-hadad's servants pictured.

explanations.answer: Send a storm to scatter both armies
explanations.explanation: A storm makes for a dramatic scene, but this text doesn't have one. The LORD says He will deliver all this great army into Ahab's hand (1 Kings 20:28). Ahab is Israel's king, and the army belongs to Aram. No storm is mentioned.
Yes. The LORD says, “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” This victory is about who He is. It's not a pat on the back for anybody's army.
That's a reasonable guess, since gods are in the middle of this fight. But the LORD never says it. What He says is, “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” The point is who He is.

The Israelite army looks like two small flocks of goats, so I'd be careful with strong. The LORD says what He will do: “I will deliver all this great army into your hand.” Then He says why: “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” It's about Him.
True. After seven days of camping across from each other, the battle ensues on the seventh day. Israel strikes down the Arameans, a hundred thousand foot soldiers in one day (1 Kings 20:29).

Close, but it's the other way around. The text says on the seventh day the battle ensued, and the Israelites struck down the Arameans. That's a hundred thousand foot soldiers in one day (1 Kings 20:29).

An inner room, friend. After the wall falls, Ben-hadad, king of Aram, flees into the city and hides there. I spent years hiding in the back of a junk drawer, so I know the instinct. I just didn't have an army to lose first.
A cave would be a classic hiding spot. But the text says Ben-hadad, Aram's king, fled to the city of Aphek and hid in an inner room. Verse 30 has no cave in it.

A tower sounds like something a king would pick. The text puts Ben-hadad, king of Aram, in an inner room in the city, though. He flees there after the Arameans lose (1 Kings 20:30). No tower is mentioned.
That's what they say. The servants tell Ben-hadad, “we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful.” That's their hope, and they build a whole plan on it.

Ruthless is the opposite of what the servants hope for. They tell Ben-hadad, king of Aram, “we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful.” Nobody builds a plan around begging for mercy from ruthless kings.
The servants don't say greedy. What they've heard is that “the kings of the house of Israel are merciful.” That's why they think Ahab might spare Ben-hadad's life.
That would be a different plan, and a loud one. The servants say they'll go out “with sackcloth around our waists and ropes around our heads.” That's not battle gear, friend. It's the opposite.

False is right. The servants say, “Let us go out to the king of Israel with sackcloth around our waists and ropes around our heads.” They don't dress for battle. They want Ahab to spare Ben-hadad's life (1 Kings 20:31).

explanations.answer: Quickly grab hold of that word
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The men were looking for a sign of hope, and they quickly grasped at the word brother. Then they answered, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad.” They didn't waste a second.

explanations.answer: Ask Ahab to say it again
explanations.explanation: Asking for a repeat is a smart move, but the text doesn't have it. The men were looking for a sign of hope, and they quickly grasped at the word. They answered right away, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad.”
Hurrying back sounds reasonable, but the men stay put. They answer Ahab on the spot, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad.” Then Ahab says, “Go and get him!”

True, and it's a surprise. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, comes out, and Ahab has him come up into his chariot (1 Kings 20:33). A king who was hiding in an inner room is now sitting next to the king who beat him.
I get why this would seem false, because it's a strange scene. But the text says Ben-hadad came out, and Ahab had him come up into his chariot. Ahab is Israel's king, and Ben-hadad is Aram's king.

explanations.answer: Makes a treaty and sends him away
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. Ahab says, “By this treaty I release you.” Then the text says, “So he made a treaty with him and sent him away.” Keep that in mind, because the story isn't done with this decision.

explanations.answer: Keeps him as a prisoner in Samaria
explanations.explanation: A prisoner in Samaria is not what happens. Ahab says to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, “By this treaty I release you.” Then he makes a treaty and sends him away (1 Kings 20:34). Ben-hadad walks out free.

explanations.answer: Hands him over to the man of God
explanations.explanation: The man of God doesn't get Ben-hadad in this scene. Ahab makes a treaty with Ben-hadad, king of Aram, and sends him away. His words are, “By this treaty I release you” (1 Kings 20:34).
I can see why you'd expect a yes, since the request came by the word of the LORD. But the text says, “the man refused to strike him.” The companion of the prophet says no.
False is right. One of the sons of the prophets says to his companion, “Strike me, please!” and the text says, “the man refused to strike him.” That refusal matters in the very next verse.

explanations.answer: Obeyed the voice of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the prophet gives. He says, “Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, as soon as you depart from me a lion will kill you.” It's a heavy moment, friend. The request came by the word of the LORD, and the companion didn't do it.
Secrets aren't part of this. The prophet says, “Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD.” That's the reason he gives for the lion in verse 36.
The text never says anything about prayer here. The prophet's words are, “Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD.” That's what the companion hasn't done.
True. The prophet finds another man and says, “Strike me, please!” This time, “the man struck him and wounded him.” That's the opposite of what the first man did.
That's what happened with the first man, but not the second. The prophet finds another man and says, “Strike me, please!” Then the text says, “the man struck him and wounded him.”
A bandage over his eyes. The prophet is wounded and waits on the road for the king, so a bandage fits the part. Disguises don't get much simpler than that.

A helmet would work for a battlefield story, and the prophet's tale does take place in the middle of a battle. But the text says he disguised himself with a bandage over his eyes (1 Kings 20:38). He's waiting for the king on the road.

A hood is a classic disguise, I'll give you that. The text has something different, though. The prophet disguises himself with a bandage over his eyes while he waits on the road for the king (1 Kings 20:38).

A talent of silver. The man tells the prophet, “Guard this man! If he goes missing for any reason, your life will be exchanged for his life, or you will weigh out a talent of silver.” That was the warning in the story the prophet tells Ahab.

A shekel is a real unit of weight, but it's not the one in this verse. The man says the prophet's life will be exchanged for the captive's life, “or you will weigh out a talent of silver.” The text says talent.
A mina is a fair guess if you know your weights. But this verse says talent. The man says, “or you will weigh out a talent of silver” (1 Kings 20:39).
I get the hope for a happy ending. But Ahab says no such thing. He says, “So shall your judgment be; you have pronounced it on yourself.” He doesn't let the prophet go free.
That's it. Ahab answers the prophet, “So shall your judgment be; you have pronounced it on yourself.” He doesn't say free. He says the judgment stands.

explanations.answer: The man God had devoted to destruction
explanations.explanation: That's what the prophet says. The word from the LORD is, “Because you have let slip from your hand the man I had devoted to destruction…” The prophet's story was about a captive. Now we hear what it was really about.

explanations.answer: The cities Aram took from his father
explanations.explanation: The cities came up when Ben-hadad, king of Aram, offered to restore them. But the LORD's word is about something else. It says Ahab let slip from his hand “the man I had devoted to destruction.”

explanations.answer: The silver his army won in battle
explanations.explanation: Silver came up in the prophet's story about a captive. The LORD's word to Ahab, Israel's king, is not about silver. He says, “Because you have let slip from your hand the man I had devoted to destruction.”
That's the second half of the word. The LORD says, “your life will be exchanged for his life, and your people for his people.” It's heavy, friend. The word is about more than Ahab alone.
Cities came up when Ben-hadad offered to restore them, but they aren't in this word. The LORD says, “your life will be exchanged for his life, and your people for his people.” It's people for people.

Silver was part of the prophet's story, but it isn't in the LORD's word to Ahab. He says, “your life will be exchanged for his life, and your people for his people.” The exchange is people for people (1 Kings 20:42).

That's how the text puts it. Ahab, Israel's king, heard the word from the LORD and went home to Samaria sullen and angry (1 Kings 20:43). I think that's a king who heard something he didn't want to hear.
Humble and sorry would be a different ending, but the text doesn't give us that. It says the king of Israel went home to Samaria sullen and angry. That's all verse 43 tells us about how he left.
Calm and thankful isn't what the text says. After the prophet's word, Ahab, Israel's king, goes home to Samaria sullen and angry (1 Kings 20:43). That's the picture we're left with.
